chapter: Leaving New York, jazz styles and religion
title: Henderson's full dance arrangements versus Ellington
summary: Smith preferred Fletcher Henderson's full arrangements for dancing and Duke for listening, and cites Talk of the Town.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Talking about Duke, and as you say, the peculiar ways in which he voiced instruments to get a particular sound...
When you were starting to arrange and being influenced in arranging, why was it that you didn't (apparently) listen as much to Duke as you did to Fletcher Henderson?
The Fletcher Henderson Band was more full.
You preferred the Fletcher way of writing?

Yeah. For dance arrangements. For dance arrangements. He didn't have no vacant spots in his arrangements. They was all full. If the reeds ain't doin' something, the brass is doin' something. If the brass is playing
one thing, the reeds are playing another. Right on it. Yeah. Ain't nothin' but space(?). That's the reason I liked it, especially for dancing.

For sweet stuff, something to sit and listen to, with all that weird voicing and weird sound, I prefer Duke. Fletcher, I'd hardly ever hear him play no sweet. Now, on "Talk Of The Town," Coleman Hawkins solo on that is one of the prettiest things you ever heard. He put the ...(?).. in D, that's the reason it sounds so pretty.
Oh, you mean you put it in the key of D.
Yeah, he put it in the key of D. That way it sounds so (?) weird, and gave it to Coleman Hawkins. Wrote right around him. Yeah, "Talk of the Town."
And a great many-many musicians tried to copy off of Coleman.
